issues.passage: The minority position can prevail only if every delegate refuses to consider it.
issues.why: "Can prevail" is correct, natural use of prevail = prove more powerful / succeed. The only-if clause is merely a paradoxical political condition; it does not make the word itself a misuse. A student who knows the definition would accept this sentence as correct English.

fix.correctPassage: Despite early resistance, the reform proposal eventually prevailed in the full assembly vote.
wrongPassages: After the motion failed on a unanimous voice vote, the chair still declared that it had prevailed.
Support for the obsolete rule began to prevail only once every jurisdiction had repealed it.
She hoped to prevail the draft simply by leaving it unread on the chair's desk.

issues.passage: Order will prevail in the hearing once interruptions drown out every measured reply.
issues.why: "Order will prevail" is a correct collocation and valid use of prevail = become widespread / prove dominant. The "once interruptions drown out…" clause is only pragmatically ironic; the word itself is not misused. A careful reader would accept the sentence as correct English (or as a wrong prediction), not as a vocab error.
